questions.q: How does SNAPSHOT isolation fundamentally differ from READ UNCOMMITTED through SERIALIZABLE?
options: It only works on single-row tables
It uses row versioning to give a consistent point-in-time view, instead of using locks to block other sessions
It disables transactions entirely
It is actually looser than READ UNCOMMITTED
questions.explain: SNAPSHOT is optimistic: instead of locking rows to prevent conflicts, it reconstructs a consistent version of the data as of the transaction's start.

questions.q: What must be done before any session can SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT?
options: Every table in the database must be rebuilt with a rowversion column
The database must have ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION turned ON
SERIALIZABLE must be enabled first
All other sessions must be disconnected
questions.explain: ALTER DATABASE ... SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON is a one-time, database-level prerequisite for SNAPSHOT isolation to be usable.

questions.q: Why don't SNAPSHOT readers block writers, or writers block SNAPSHOT readers?
options: SNAPSHOT isolation disables all locks database-wide for every session
A SNAPSHOT read is served from a versioned copy of the data, not the live row, so there's no shared lock for a writer to wait on
Writers always wait for SNAPSHOT readers to finish, just silently
SNAPSHOT isolation only reads from a separate read-only replica
questions.explain: Because SNAPSHOT reads a versioned, consistent copy rather than the live row under lock, there's nothing for a concurrent writer to block on, and vice versa.

questions.q: What happens when two SNAPSHOT transactions both try to update the same row, based on the same starting snapshot?
options: The first transaction to start automatically blocks the second from even reading the row
Both updates silently succeed, and the last one wins with no error
SQL Server raises error 3960 and rolls back the second transaction to commit its write
SQL Server merges both updates into a single combined value
questions.explain: SNAPSHOT isolation detects this write-write conflict and aborts the second writer with error 3960, rather than letting it silently overwrite based on stale data.

questions.q: If Window 1 opens a SNAPSHOT transaction and reads a row, then Window 2 updates and commits a change to that same row under READ COMMITTED, what does Window 1 see on a second read of that row (still in its original transaction)?
options: NULL, because the row is now ambiguous
Window 2's new value, because SNAPSHOT always shows the latest committed data
An error, because the row was modified by another session
The original value, because Window 1 is reading from its own fixed snapshot taken at the transaction's start
questions.explain: SNAPSHOT isolation gives a consistent view of the data as of when the transaction started, unaffected by other transactions committing afterward.
